idiom_name: XState createMachine + one actor per instance with persisted snapshots
implementation_notes: XState gives the decider as a serialisable machine: states, guarded transitions, delayed transitions (after) for deadlines and invoked or spawned actors for the steps, while one actor per process instance holds the state and a snapshot can be persisted and rehydrated from a database row. Persistence and delivery guarantees remain yours - store the snapshot atomically with the outgoing command and make the step handlers idempotent, because the transport repeats messages. The hand-written alternative (a status column plus a switch and a job queue) is still common in small services where the dependency is unwanted; choose XState when the flow has several states and timers and you want them visible in one definition.
pitfalls: Snapshots are coupled to the machine's id and shape: rehydrating an instance after the definition was edited silently misinterprets persisted state unless the version is checked.
Delayed transitions (after) live in memory; when the process restarts before the delay fires the timeout never happens, so deadlines must also be stored and re-armed.
Invoked actors and forwarded events keep subscriptions alive; an actor that is stopped without stopping its children leaks handlers and can process replies for a dead instance.
Using a timer that keeps the Node process alive (setTimeout without unref and without cancellation) turns a forgotten deadline into a shutdown problem.
